payload.text: Wind and solar farms now produce electricity more cheaply than almost any {{b1}} plant, but they do so on their own timetable. The difficulty is no longer generation; it is {{b2}}. Batteries can hold a few hours of supply, enough to carry a city through the evening peak, yet a still, grey week in winter demands something far larger. Pumped hydro remains the cheapest answer wherever the {{b3}} allows it, and several countries are testing tanks of hot rock and compressed air. None of this will matter, though, unless the grid itself is rebuilt to move power from where the wind {{b4}} to where the people live.

payload.title: The Ward That Turned the Volume Down
paragraphs: An intensive care unit is one of the loudest rooms in which anybody is ever asked to sleep. Monitors beep, pumps click, doors swing and staff talk across the beds through the night. Measurements taken in several European hospitals put the average night-time level at around sixty decibels, roughly that of a busy restaurant, with peaks far above it. A ceiling of thirty-five decibels has been recommended for wards since the late 1990s; almost none of the units in the study came close, and the noisiest hours fell between two and four in the morning.

Patients notice, and so do their bodies. Sleep on a ward arrives in short fragments, and the deep stages that repair tissue and settle the immune system often never come at all. Researchers have linked this to slower healing, larger doses of painkillers and the confused, agitated state that is common in older patients after surgery. Staff, by contrast, stop hearing the noise entirely. Alarms sound so frequently that the great majority turn out to be false, and a nurse who has silenced forty of them since midnight will be slower to reach the one that matters.

The measures that work are unglamorous. One Dutch hospital fitted soft-closing lids to its bins, moved the shift handover away from the bedsides and set every non-urgent alarm to flash rather than sound; night-time levels fell by nine decibels within a month. Acoustic ceilings and single rooms achieve more, but they are paid for once, when a building goes up, and most of the wards in use today were drawn up at a time when quiet was thought of as a courtesy rather than as part of the treatment.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Hospital wards are far noisier than the guidelines allow, and the noise harms patients' recovery and dulls staff's response to alarms, although cheap changes to routines and equipment can reduce it.
Intensive care units have become quieter than busy restaurants since the thirty-five decibel guideline was introduced in the late 1990s.
The main cause of noise on hospital wards is patients themselves, who talk and move about during the night and disturb one another.
Only hospitals with acoustic ceilings and single rooms can meet the recommended night-time noise levels, so older buildings should be replaced.

questions.before: Nurses become slower to answer alarms because
questions.after: and so the single alarm that signals a real emergency may not be reached in time.
options: so many of the alarms turn out to be false
the alarms are set at a volume that is too low to hear
patients regularly ask them to switch the alarms off
the monitors are turned off between two and four in the morning

questions.prompt: 高価な建物の改修ではなく、日々の習慣を変えることで騒音を減らせることを最もよく示している語句はどれですか。

spans.text: put the average night-time level at around sixty decibels
the deep stages that repair tissue and settle the immune system
moved the shift handover away from the bedsides
most of the wards in use today were drawn up

questions.sentence: The trouble, in other words, is not only that the ward is loud but that the people working in it have stopped hearing how loud it is.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Quiet should be treated as part of a patient's treatment rather than as a politeness, and much of it can be won by changing routines and equipment instead of waiting for new buildings.
Hospitals should remove alarms from intensive care units altogether, since almost all of them are false and none of the staff respond to them anyway.
Noise levels in wards matter mainly because they make the work of nurses unpleasant, not because they have any effect on how patients recover.
Because the thirty-five decibel guideline is impossible to meet in practice, it should be raised to match the sixty decibels that wards actually reach.

payload.title: Reading the Air Trapped in Ice
paragraphs: Every winter, snow falls on the middle of Greenland and never melts. Each layer presses down on the ones beneath it, and the air caught between the flakes is slowly sealed into bubbles. A drill can lift out a column of that ice three kilometres long, and the lowest metre of it froze long before anyone planted the first field of wheat. Every bubble is a small, dated sample of the atmosphere itself, which is why a piece of ice can answer questions that no written record can.

The dating is the delicate part. Near the surface, annual layers can be counted rather like tree rings, using the dust that blows in each spring. Further down, the layers are squeezed to the thickness of a page and simple counting fails, so researchers match volcanic ash and sudden chemical spikes to eruptions whose dates are already known from elsewhere. An error of only a few years at a depth of fifty thousand years is regarded as a good result, and every claim about how quickly the climate once changed rests on that accuracy.

What the bubbles show is that carbon dioxide and temperature have risen and fallen together for at least eight hundred thousand years, within a band that the present century has already left far behind. The ice also records how fast the system can turn: at the end of the last ice age, Greenland warmed by something close to ten degrees within a single human lifetime. Cores from mountain glaciers, which hold the most recent centuries in the finest detail, are the ones now vanishing fastest, and several teams are drilling simply to store the ice in freezers before it is gone.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Ice cores preserve dated samples of ancient air, and although dating them deep down is difficult, they reveal both the long link between carbon dioxide and temperature and how abruptly the climate can shift.
Drilling in Greenland has shown that carbon dioxide levels have stayed inside the same narrow band throughout the present century.
Counting annual layers in ice is as straightforward as counting the rings of a tree, whatever the depth of the core.
Mountain glaciers are melting so quickly that ice cores can no longer be used as a record of the atmosphere.

questions.before: Counting yearly layers becomes impossible deep inside a core because
questions.after: so researchers rely instead on ash from eruptions whose dates are already known.
options: the pressure squeezes the layers until they are far too thin to separate
the ice at that depth contains no trapped air at all
the dust that marks each spring never reaches central Greenland
the drill destroys the lower part of the column as it turns

questions.prompt: 気候が人ひとりの一生ほどの短い間に大きく変わりうることを最もよく示している語句はどれですか。

spans.text: the air caught between the flakes is slowly sealed into bubbles
An error of only a few years at a depth of fifty thousand years
Greenland warmed by something close to ten degrees within a single human lifetime
several teams are drilling simply to store the ice in freezers

questions.sentence: Nothing else keeps the air itself; a fossil or a tree ring can only record what that air did to something living.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Ice is the only archive that holds ancient air directly, and reading it carefully shows both a long partnership between carbon dioxide and temperature and a capacity for very sudden change — which is why the melting cores are being rescued.
Because dating errors of a few years are unavoidable, conclusions drawn from ice cores about past climate change should be treated as guesswork.
The main value of ice cores is that they let scientists predict exactly when the next ice age will begin and how long it will last.
Storing glacier ice in freezers has become unnecessary now that mountain cores have all been drilled and measured.
